title: the summit sit
hook: rain, a dark narrow shelter, three strangers pressed together, and then a fourth who wasn't there before

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit went back to karma and seva, and a king who gave away his last cup of water. Did you do one small job whose fruit went to someone else, and keep quiet about it? Day one thousand four hundred eighteen.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `THE LAST CUP OF WATER.`

segments.voice: Rain is coming down hard at night. A wandering devotee ducks into a tiny shelter by a house. A second traveler knocks, and the first makes room. A third arrives, soaked, and the two make room again, so now they're standing shoulder to shoulder in the dark. And then, tradition says, they feel a fourth pressing in among them, someone none of them can see. That's the story told of the first Alvars, the Tamil singers of Vishnu. Today's summit sit climbs back to the bhakti stretch of the lineage track, and the lamps those three lit in the dark.
screen: `RAIN, AND A TINY SHELTER.` → `ROOM MADE, AND MADE AGAIN.` → `A FOURTH, PRESSING IN.`

segments.voice: In the story, each of them sings a verse to light the dark. The first, Poygai, makes a lamp out of the world: the earth for its bowl, the ocean for its oil, the sun for its flame. The second, Bhutam, makes a lamp out of the heart: love for the bowl, longing for the oil, a melting mind for the wick. And the third, Pey, by that light, says simply: I have seen. The Lord is there, with the goddess, in the crowded dark. Now hold that next to the Narada Bhakti Sutras, the short book the year read whole. Its boldest claim is that bhakti, love for God, isn't the road to something else. It is where the road goes. Love is its own fruit. And when the sutras try to say what that love is like, they give up gracefully: it can't be told, they say, like a taste in the mouth of someone who can't speak. You can have it. You can't hand it over in words. From up here, the shelter and the sutras are telling the same thing in different keys. The singers don't argue their way to God. They light lamps and look. And the lamps are made of what they already have: the whole world, for one of them, and their own love, for another. Then think back to the women of the bhakti stretch later in the year, and the singers of the regions: a tailor, a cobbler, a weaver, singing to God in a home language. The shelter was too small. They made room anyway. And that, the story says, is when God pressed in.
screen: `A LAMP MADE OF THE WORLD.` · `A LAMP MADE OF LOVE.` · `LOVE IS ITS OWN FRUIT.` · `A TASTE THAT CAN'T BE TOLD.` · then, large: `THEY MADE ROOM ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: making room. Sit, and let the breath settle. Notice how full the mind is, the way the shelter was full. Don't push anything out. Just, on each out-breath, make a little room, the way the first traveler shifted over for the second. Notice whether the chest feels a little wider. If you pray, you can let that room be for God, the way the Alvars felt someone press in. If you don't, let it be room for whoever comes next today. The bell holds the time.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: bhakti, the Alvars' lamps in a crowded shelter, and a love the sutras call its own fruit. Today's word.
Your line: the summit sit. Today, when a space is already crowded, a table, a bench, a conversation, make room for one more. Day one thousand four hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: The hymns of the Alvars are sung in Sri Vaishnava temples and homes in Tamil Nadu, and the Narada Bhakti Sutras are studied and recited by devotees of many bhakti traditions.

fork.setup: you're sheltering from the rain in a space that barely fits two. a third traveler knocks, soaked. what do you do?
options: go back out into the rain.
fork.reveal: in the story, they make room and stand together. then they feel a fourth press in among them, and each sings a lamp into the dark.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: bhakti, devotion, love for God.

trapdoor: what you thought: bhakti is a way to earn God's favor.
what it means: in the Narada Bhakti Sutras, love for God is its own fruit, not a road to something else.
what a scholar hears: the first verses of the Mudal, Irandam and Munram Tiruvantati, which tradition says Poygai, Bhutam and Pey sang together in the shelter at Tirukkovalur.

Story of the first Alvars at Tirukkovalur

notes: Summit sit, day 7: revisits 'bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete' (1214–1219) and 'the Alvar hymns' (1220–1225). The Tirukkovalur shelter story was the hook of 1223; this day uses it as the frame and adds the sutras.

The shelter story is told as tradition; the voice avoids the traditional 'room for one to lie, two to sit, three to stand' to keep numbers out of the claims. The order of arrival (Poygai, Bhutam, Pey) and the presence of Vishnu with Lakshmi: confirm.
Opening verses paraphrased: Poygai (earth as bowl, ocean as ghee, sun as flame), Bhutam (love as bowl, longing as ghee, melting mind as wick), Pey (I have seen: the Lord with Sri). Confirm.
Narada Bhakti Sutras: bhakti as supreme love (2); its own fruit (26, 30); its nature indescribable, like the taste of a mute (51–52). Sutra numbers vary between editions; confirm.
'The short book the year read whole' refers to the outline's 'complete'; confirm the 1214–1219 days did cover the whole text.
Editor pass: 'how often … from people with very little' replaced by the year's own named singers (tailor, cobbler, weaver); the practice no longer tells the listener what to feel.
